evidence_quotes.quote: The majority of households we surveyed in Kejetia (77.8 percent) obtain at least some of their water from water vendors. Over half (55.6 percent) of households exclusively purchase water from vendors.

In an area without government provision of water, this situation has also forced community members to develop innovative water strategies that reflect the ways that water is understood and valued with regard to personal health and the environment as well as to the seasonality of water acquisition.

Indeed, one might say that government oversight over water access and use does not exist in Kejetia. Preferred sources of drinking water (pipeborne or borehole water) are not available at the mining site
With the open-ended questionnaire, we interviewed 20 individuals associated with the water trade in Kejetia. We also interviewed five women in the community about their household water use.
Obtaining water in Kejetia also takes more time than other parts of Ghana. Over 70 percent of households surveyed in Kejetia take 30 or more minutes to obtain drinking water

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community drinking and domestic water access, procurement strategies, water vending, and lack of public water and sanitation infrastructure in Kejetia, a small-scale gold mining community in Talensi District, Upper East Region, Ghana.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2 ('institutional, regulatory or governance factor') because the paper discusses local government neglect and lack of political representation in transient registered mining concessions compared with a settled village (Gorogo) and documents informal community stream-protection prohibitions, private well/mine-pump access stipulations, and water-vendor price-fixing meetings (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include'). However, it FAILS the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism reading (c2 = 'no'): formal government oversight and public water provision do not exist at the site and are treated only as unanalysed macro-governance background, while the empirical study examines sociocultural/sensory vs. chemical valuations of water, artisanal gold-mining contamination, and informal surface-water/mine-pit vending rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, or utility rule-type mechanism governing service access (eligibility screening, documentation/tenure rules, formal tariffs, administrative burden, discretion, regulatory enforcement, or utility structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical evidence from June-July 2011 (and 2010-2011 water sampling): a cluster-sampled household survey (n=54 households), open-ended interviews with 20 water-trade actors and 5 community women, participant observation, and laboratory heavy-metal and coliform testing of water samples from Kejetia and a control village (Gorogo).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports household water access outcomes including main and all water sources for drinking, cooking, hand-washing, and laundering (69.8% surface water and 30.2% sachet water as main drinking sources; 0% main borehole/piped water), water collection time (>70% of households taking 30 or more minutes), reliance on water vendors (77.8% some water; 55.6% exclusively), and informal water prices ($0.03 median, $0.12-$0.29 vendor-reported price per 34-liter basin), alongside chemical water quality.
criterion_notes.c5: Clearly identifies the population and units of analysis (54 surveyed households and 25 interviewees in Kejetia, plus water samples from Kejetia and control village Gorogo), the empirical exposure/context examined by the authors (small-scale gold mining environment, water source types, and sociocultural/economic valuation in an unserved community), the water access and chemical quality outcomes, and the cross-sectional mixed-methods study design.

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed-methods study (cluster household survey, semi-structured interviews, participant observation, and environmental water quality sampling)
population_and_sample: 54 cluster-sampled households (1 adult per household), 20 informal water-trade workers (water vendors, bathhouse workers, pito brewers), and 5 women interviewed in Kejetia small-scale gold mining community, Talensi District, Upper East Region, Ghana, plus water samples from Kejetia and control village Gorogo
exposure: Small-scale gold mining community context, water source types (stream, abandoned mine-pits, sachet, rainwater, private mine pump), and sociocultural/sensory water valuation in an area without government water provision
outcome: Household drinking and domestic water source distribution, time to obtain drinking water (>=30 minutes), reliance on informal water vendors, informal basin prices, and heavy-metal/coliform water contamination
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While this empirical mixed-methods study examines household drinking and domestic water access, vendor reliance, collection time, and heavy-metal contamination in a Ghanaian small-scale gold mining community (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), it does not empirically examine a rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or utility mechanism governing water or sanitation service access. Formal government water provision and oversight are absent in Kejetia and appear only as unanalysed macro-governance background, while the empirical analysis focuses on sociocultural/sensory perceptions of water quality, informal surface-water/mine-pit vending and hygiene etiquette, and chemical metal concentrations. Under the literal/broad plain wording of Criterion 2, the discussion of local government neglect of transient mining concessions and informal community/vendor water rules would pass (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include').
